title: St. Elmo's fire
description: Luminous plasma created in an electric field
wiki_lead:
St. Elmo's fire (also called corposant, Hermes fire, furole, witchfire or witch's fire) is a weather phenomenon in which luminous plasma is created by a corona discharge from a rod-like object such as a mast, spire, chimney, or animal horn in an atmospheric electric field. It has also been observed on the leading edges and windshields of aircraft  by pilots. 
The intensity of the effect, a blue or violet glow around the object, often accompanied by a hissing or buzzing sound, is proportional to the strength of the electric field and therefore noticeable primarily during thunderstorms or volcanic eruptions.
St. Elmo's fire is named after St. Erasmus of Formia (also known as St. Elmo), the patron saint of sailors. The phenomenon, which can warn of an imminent lightning strike, was regarded by sailors with awe and sometimes considered to be a good omen.

Cause
St. Elmo's fire is a reproducible and demonstrable form of plasma. The electric field around the affected object causes ionization of the air molecules, producing a faint glow easily visible in low-light conditions. Conditions that can generate St. Elmo's fire are present during thunderstorms, when high-voltage differentials are present between clouds and the ground underneath. A local electric field of about 100 kV/m is required to begin an electric discharge in moist air. The magnitude of the electric field depends greatly on the geometry (shape and size) of the object. Sharp points lower the necessary voltage because electric fields are more concentrated in areas of high curvature, so discharges preferentially occur and are more intense at the ends of pointed objects.
The nitrogen and oxygen in the Earth's atmosphere cause St. Elmo's fire to emit blue or violet light via the same kind of mechanism that causes clear neon gas-discharge lamps to glow (without phosphors), albeit with a different colour due to the different gases involved.
In 1751, Benjamin Franklin hypothesized that a pointed iron rod would light up at the tip during a lightning storm, similar in appearance to St. Elmo's fire.
In an August 2020 paper, researchers in MIT's Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics demonstrated that St. Elmo's fire behaves differently in airborne objects versus grounded structures. They show that electrically isolated structures accumulate charge more effectively in high wind, in contrast to the corona discharge observed in grounded structures.

grok_lead: St. Elmo's fire is a luminous electrical phenomenon characterized by a colorful plasma glow or brush-like discharge that forms around pointed objects, such as ship masts or aircraft wings, when they are exposed to a strong atmospheric electric field during thunderstorms. This corona discharge occurs as the intense electric field ionizes surrounding air molecules, accelerating electrons that collide with atoms to produce visible light, often in shades of blue, violet, or other hues resembling a neon sign. Unlike lightning, it is a continuous, low-energy glow rather than a sudden spark, though it can signal the presence of nearby lightning risks. Historically, the phenomenon has been observed and interpreted by sailors since ancient times, often viewed as a supernatural sign due to its eerie appearance in stormy conditions. It derives its name from St. Erasmus of Formia, known as St. Elmo in Italian tradition, the patron saint of Mediterranean sailors, who believed the light signified divine protection or the end of a storm. Early accounts, including those from Greek and Roman mariners associating it with the twin gods Castor and Pollux, highlight its role as both a good omen of safety and a warning of peril, with the glow sometimes accompanied by a hissing sound. In modern contexts, St. Elmo's fire remains a notable hazard and spectacle for aviators and seafarers, frequently reported on aircraft during turbulent weather, where it may appear on wingtips or propellers without causing damage but indicating high electrical activity. Scientific understanding emphasizes its formation through dielectric breakdown of air at field strengths around 3 megavolts per meter, making it a visible example of atmospheric electricity in action.
